stops.name: Grüningen, the vigil at Sophie's sickbed and her death
stops.campa: Sophie sickens with a liver-tumour; three cruel operations between the spring and summer of 1796 fail to save her. Friedrich watches her waste. On 19 March 1797, two days after her fifteenth birthday, she dies. The betrothed of a child-bride is left standing in a wrecked world, half in love with following her. Within months his beloved brother Erasmus dies too of consumption. Grief closes over him like water, and out of that water, impossibly, a new sun will rise.

stops.name: The grave-mound at Kirchberg, Grüningen: the vision of 13 May 1797
stops.campa: On the evening of 13 May he rides to her grave on the Kirchberg. He stands alone by the barren mound that hides the vanished form of his life, powerless, nothing but conscious misery. And then it comes. Out of the blue distances a shiver of twilight breaks; the chains of daylight snap; the glory of the world flees and his mourning with it. The mound becomes a cloud of dust, and through it he sees the glorified face of the beloved. Death is not the end but the bride; the Night more holy than the Day. Grief is transmuted into gospel: the Hymns to the Night are born.
stops.quote: Once when I was shedding bitter tears... I stood alone by the barren mound which in its narrow dark bosom hid the vanished form of my life... then, out of the blue distances — from the hills of my ancient bliss, came a shiver of twilight... Away fled the glory of the world, and with it my mourning... The mound became a cloud of dust — and through the cloud I saw the glorified face of my beloved.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Hymns to the Night, Third Hymn (trans. George MacDonald), from the diary entry of 13 May 1797

stops.name: Freiberg, the Bergakademie under Abraham Gottlob Werner
stops.campa: At the end of 1797, still raw with grief, he enrols at the Bergakademie Freiberg, the world's oldest mining school, to qualify for the salt service. Under the great geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner he descends into the science of the deep earth: strata, ores, the Neptunist history of rock, but also galvanism, chemistry, mathematics, medicine. In him geology becomes mysticism: the mine a temple, the miner a priest of the interior, the earth a living cipher. The poet learns to read the crust of the planet as a book.
stops.quote: Es gibt eigne Bergleute, die geboren sind, den verborgenen Schätzen der Natur nachzuspüren.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Heinrich von Ofterdingen (the miner's tale), echoing his Freiberg years

stops.name: The Freiberg mines: the descent, and The Novices of Sais
stops.campa: He goes down into the working shafts of the Freiberg silver-country, lamp in hand, into galleries where the earth's secret writing is exposed. The mine becomes for him a sanctuary: the miner a still, humble priest who seeks not gold but knowledge, at home in the dark as others are in the light. Out of these descents grows his unfinished tale The Novices of Sais: the veiled goddess Nature, whom the initiate longs to unveil, and finds, lifting the veil, his own beloved. Geology has become a mystery-religion.
stops.quote: Einem gelang es — er hob den Schleier der Göttin zu Sais. Aber was sah er? er sah — Wunder des Wunders — sich selbst.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Die Lehrlinge zu Sais (The Novices of Sais)

stops.name: Weimar, visiting Goethe and August Wilhelm Schlegel
stops.campa: Travelling in these Freiberg years, he passes through Weimar and pays court to the great ones: Goethe, whom he reveres and resists in equal measure, and August Wilhelm Schlegel. He meets Schelling; he calls on Jean Paul in Leipzig. The unknown salt-auditor is being drawn into the constellation of German letters. In 1798 his fragments appear in the Schlegels' journal Athenäum under a new name taken from an old Hardenberg title: Novalis, 'the clearer of new land.' The poet has christened himself.

stops.name: Dresden, the picture gallery and the Sistine Madonna
stops.campa: In the summer the Schlegels call him to Dresden to walk the great picture gallery with them. There, before Raphael's Sistine Madonna, the young Romantics stand transfigured: the Virgin becomes for them the image of a redeeming, universal humanity, art itself a kind of scripture. Novalis, still steeped in the Night and the lost Sophie, sees in the painted Mother the same holy feminine that haunts his hymns. The gallery is a temple; the sacred and the aesthetic fuse. He carries the vision back to his notebooks and his coming Spiritual Songs.

stops.name: Teplitz (Teplice, Bohemia), the Teplitz Fragments
stops.campa: Between his labours he takes the waters at Teplitz in Bohemia, and there fills a notebook with the Teplitz Fragments: over a hundred aphorisms on love, faith, the feminine, the state, and everyday life. It is his encyclopaedic dream in miniature: to think all knowledge together, to 'romanticize' the world by giving the commonplace a high meaning and the mysterious a familiar face. The salt-official spa-guest is quietly composing a whole philosophy on the backs of loose sheets.
stops.quote: Die Welt muss romantisirt werden. So findet man den ursprünglichen Sinn wieder.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Fragments (the programme of 'romanticizing' the world)

stops.name: Freiberg: the second betrothal, to Julie von Charpentier
stops.campa: In December, at Freiberg, life reaches again for the living: he becomes engaged a second time, to Julie von Charpentier, daughter of the mining-professor Johann von Charpentier. It is a gentler, more earthly love than the consuming vision of Sophie: a promise of an ordinary future, marriage, a career in the salt-works. He does not renounce the Night; he means to serve the Day as well. But the consumption already stirring in his lungs will not let him keep both.

stops.name: Weissenfels: assessor of the salt-works; the Spiritual Songs
stops.campa: His studies done, he returns to Weissenfels and is made assessor, then director, of the electoral salt-works: a serious young official who inspects mines and reckons brine, and who at his desk by candlelight writes the Geistliche Lieder, the Spiritual Songs. In them the erotic mysticism of the Night turns openly Christian: Mary, the Eucharist, the sweetness of the Redeemer. The engineer of salt is also the hymnodist of a new, tender, Romantic faith.
stops.quote: Wenn ich ihn nur habe, / Wenn er mein nur ist... / Weiß ich nichts von Leide, / Fühle nichts, als Andacht, Lieb und Freude.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Geistliche Lieder (Spiritual Songs), No. 5, first stanza

stops.name: Jena: the meeting with Ludwig Tieck; beginning Heinrich von Ofterdingen
stops.campa: In the summer he comes to Jena and meets Ludwig Tieck, and a last great friendship opens. Tieck lends him Jakob Böhme, the shoemaker-mystic; the two talk of a poetry that would make the world magical again. Fired, Novalis begins his novel Heinrich von Ofterdingen. Its young hero lies dreaming and longs, above all treasure, to behold the blaue Blume, the blue flower, the flower of infinite longing that will become the emblem of Romanticism itself, of every unappeasable desire in the world.
stops.quote: Nicht die Schätze sind es, die ein so unaussprechliches Verlangen in mir geweckt haben... aber die blaue Blume sehne ich mich zu erblicken.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Heinrich von Ofterdingen, opening chapter

stops.name: Jena, the Romantic gathering of November 1799
stops.campa: On 11 November he arrives for the famous Romantikertreffen: the gathering of the Jena circle. In the house of the Schlegels come together Friedrich and August Wilhelm Schlegel and their women Caroline and Dorothea, Ludwig Tieck, Friedrich Schelling, and Novalis. For a few electric days the founders of German Romanticism read to one another, quarrel, philosophize. Here he reads his essay Die Christenheit oder Europa, dreaming of a re-enchanted, spiritually reunited Europe, too visionary for even his friends, who advise against printing it.
stops.quote: Es waren schöne glänzende Zeiten, wo Europa ein christliches Land war, wo Eine Christenheit diesen menschlich gestalteten Welttheil bewohnte.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Die Christenheit oder Europa (Christianity or Europe), 1799

stops.name: Weissenfels, the dream of the Blue Flower written down
stops.campa: At his desk in Weissenfels he writes the opening of Heinrich von Ofterdingen. The young hero, sleepless with a stranger's tales, falls at last into a dream: a great blue flower stands by a spring, and as he bends to it the petals part and within them hovers a delicate human face. It is the beloved, it is the far-off, it is the never-attainable that draws the whole soul forward. In this single image Novalis names Romanticism itself: longing given a flower, the world made dream and the dream made world.
stops.quote: Die Welt wird Traum, der Traum wird Welt.
